questions.question: In a square assignment problem, each row $i$ is assigned exactly one column $j$ and each column is used exactly once, at cost $c_{ij}$. A constant $a_i$ is added to every cost in row $i$. Which statement is correct?
options: The optimal total cost is the same as before
The optimal assignments are the same as before
Only the optimal assignment's total rises by $a_i$
Row $i$ may now be given a different column

questions.question: In a square assignment problem, each row $i$ is assigned exactly one column $j$ and each column is used exactly once, at cost $c_{ij}$. Why does subtracting the same amount $b_j$ from every cost in column $j$ leave the best assignment unchanged?
options: Column $j$ then contains a cost of exactly zero
Every complete assignment uses column $j$ once
Subtracting keeps every cost nonnegative
The optimal assignment does not use column $j$

questions.question: For a square one-to-one assignment problem with costs $c_{ij}$, which of these changes to the costs can alter the set of optimal assignments?
options: Adding 3 to every cost $c_{1j}$ in row 1
Subtracting column 2's minimum from column 2
Adding 3 to every cost in the whole table
Adding 3 to only the single cost $c_{12}$

questions.question: A square assignment problem maximizes the total profit $\sum_ip_{i,\pi(i)}$, where $\pi(i)$ is the column assigned to row $i$. Why is each profit turned into the cost $M-p_{ij}$ with $M$ large, instead of just $-p_{ij}$?
options: To change which assignment has the highest profit
Because $-p_{ij}$ would turn the problem back into maximization
Because $M-p_{ij}$ counts each profit $n$ times
To keep the minimization's costs nonnegative

questions.question: In a square assignment problem, each row $i$ is assigned exactly one column $j$ and each column is used exactly once, at cost $c_{ij}$. After subtracting from each row its smallest cost (the row minimum), which statement about the new cost table is correct?
options: Each row and each column has a 0
Each row has a 0 and no cost is negative
The row zeros form an optimal assignment
Every complete total is unchanged

questions.question: A 3-row assignment problem maximizes profit with $P=\begin{pmatrix}6&9&4\\8&5&7\\3&6&9\end{pmatrix}$ (row $i$, column $j$: profit $p_{ij}$), converted to costs $9-p_{ij}$. What is the cost of the assignment $(1,2),(2,1),(3,3)$?

In a square assignment problem, each row $i$ is assigned exactly one column $j$ and each column is used exactly once, at cost $c_{ij}$, with 3 rows. A complete assignment has total 20. Then 3 is added to every cost in row 2 and 5 is subtracted from every cost in column 1. What is the assignment's new total?
From a square cost table, row and column minima are subtracted, leaving only nonnegative costs. Why is a complete assignment that uses only zeros of the reduced table optimal for the original costs?
options: No complete total in the reduced table is below 0
Zeros mark the cheapest cost of each original row
Every zero of the reduced table must be used
The reduction lowers every complete total to 0

questions.question: Adding $a_i$ to every cost in row $i$ preserves the optimal assignments when each row is used exactly once. Suppose instead some agent (row) may take two tasks (columns). Why could the same row change alter the best assignment?
options: Row changes are never allowed in such problems
Totals using row $i$ twice would rise by $2a_i$
The costs in row $i$ might then become negative
The column totals would no longer add up

questions.question: A square assignment problem with $n$ rows maximizes profit $\sum_ip_{i,\pi(i)}$, where $\pi(i)$ is row $i$'s column. Each profit is converted to cost $M-p_{ij}$. Why does minimizing total cost give the most profitable assignment?
options: Total cost is $nM-\sum_ip_{i,\pi(i)}$, falling as profit rises
Total cost equals $M-\sum_ip_{i,\pi(i)}$, so it ranks profit
Costs $M-p_{ij}$ order each row from most to least profitable
Total cost $nM+\sum_ip_{i,\pi(i)}$ is smallest when profit is

questions.question: In a square assignment problem, each row $i$ is assigned exactly one column $j$ and each column is used exactly once, at cost $c_{ij}$. Adding constants to rows and columns preserves the set of optimal assignments. Is every cost change that preserves this set of that row-and-column form?
options: No: doubling every cost also keeps the optimal set
Yes: any other change alters some total differently
Yes: only row and column changes keep costs comparable
No: changing one cost never alters the optimal set

questions.question: For the cost table $C=\begin{pmatrix}8&5&9\\6&4&9\\9&7&6\end{pmatrix}$ (row $i$ is assigned column $j$ at cost $c_{ij}$; a pair $(i,j)$ means row $i$ gets column $j$), a student subtracts 7 from every cost in row 1, although its minimum is 5, giving costs $1,-2,2$ in row 1. What happens to the optimal assignments?
options: They change, as only the minimum may be subtracted
They change, as row 1 now favours its negative cost
They stay the same, and the minimum total stays 17
They stay the same; only the nonnegativity is lost

questions.question: From a 3-row cost table $C$, row minima and then column minima, totalling 15, are subtracted, giving $R=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\0&2&1\\0&3&2\end{pmatrix}$ (row $i$ is assigned column $j$). What is the minimum total cost of a complete assignment for $C$?
